Location: `_compute_equivalence_classes` (lines ~124‑142).  
  Evidence: After clustering findings by `similarity >= tau_sim`, the code creates `FindingEquivalenceClass` objects with `flaw_class = members[0].flaw_class`. Findings with different `flaw_class` values are merged into one equivalence class if they happen to be text‑similar, and the class gets only the first member’s flaw class.  
  The equivalence class is supposed to represent a single, well‑defined flaw type.  Merging distinct flaw categories distorts all subsequent convergence metrics that rely on distinct class counts and aggregated severity.

Location: `_novel_classes` (lines ~165–191).  
  Evidence: The method iterates over equivalence classes of the current round and, for each class, checks whether any member is similar to any prior finding. If any single member matches a prior, the entire class is marked non‑novel and discarded.  
  Similarity is not transitive, so a class can contain a duplicate member A (similar to a prior X) and a genuinely novel member B (not similar to any prior) that was clustered with A because `sim(A,B) ≥ tau_sim` but `sim(B,X) < tau_sim`. In that case, B’s novelty is thrown away, under‑counting novel severity and potentially allowing the system to converge prematurely.

`_compute_equivalence_classes` (line 117) and `_novel_classes` (line 190) cluster and compare findings by textual similarity alone, ignoring `flaw_class`. The `FindingEquivalenceClass` docstring in `_types.py:489` states *"Findings are equivalent if they share flaw_class and have sim(f_i, f_j) >= tau_sim"*, but the code does not enforce the flaw_class constraint. Concrete proof: two findings with `flaw_class=1` (buffer overflow) and `flaw_class=5` (race condition) sharing keywords cluster together with Jaccard=0.52 > tau_sim=0.33. The novel flaw_class=5 finding is then suppressed as a rediscovery.
